articles.title: I asked Gemma to turn “I'm too tired” into “glad I went out” 🚶‍♀️
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: "Touch Grass" Evening comes, and after a long day I think a lot of us do the same thing: look at the front door, look…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: "Touch Grass" Evening comes, and after a long day I think a lot of us do the same thing: look at the front door, look at the sofa. The sofa wins. Not because we don't want to go out, but because after a long day, "go for a walk" sounds like one more task. But give me a tiny quest ( find the quietest sound in the street , touch something rough and tell me what it felt like , spot a tree lit up by a streetlamp ) and it stops being one more task. It becomes a reason to go out looking for something, one that can turn the day around. Some days we're drained because we didn't get much done or something didn't work out; a few small challenges are a way to switch off and unwind.

articles.title: Require an Empty Fixture Diff Before Extracting a Batch Loop
articles.excerpt: A late cleanup request arrived with a four-hundred-line diff that rewrote validation, deduplication, and persistence in one pass. The existing tests covered only the happy path, so a green CI run coul…
articles.body: A late cleanup request arrived with a four-hundred-line diff that rewrote validation, deduplication, and persistence in one pass. The existing tests covered only the happy path, so a green CI run could not explain the legacy rows. The reviewer needed a smaller change that preserved every observed output before any structural boundary was allowed to move. This composite scenario shows how to freeze those outputs, then accept only the smallest safe edit. The module under review is a batch upload normalizer that grew by successive tickets rather than by design. It reads a list of records, fills missing defaults, drops exact repeats, and writes survivors to storage. Those four jobs share one function, so a cleanup that touches all of them cannot be reviewed as one claim.

articles.title: Ideas die in the doc because the doc never argues with you. So I built one that does.
articles.excerpt: Every idea I got excited about died the same way: a Notion page with a name, a paragraph of vibes, and no first step. The doc never pushed back. So I built Shrink — one static HTML file, no signup, no…
articles.body: Every idea I got excited about died the same way: a Notion page with a name, a paragraph of vibes, and no first step. The doc never pushed back. So I built Shrink — one static HTML file, no signup, no server. It asks six questions, one at a time, and won't let you advance until the answer is actually specific. Answer all six and it prints a one-page spec you can paste anywhere. Skip one and it prints a visible hole for that question, so you can see exactly what you dodged. The six: What is it? — one sentence, no adjectives doing the work Who is it for? — a person, not a demographic What do they do today instead? — the real alternative, including "nothing" What's the smallest version that still counts as real? — shippable today What would make you kill it?

articles.title: Fine-tuning gpt-oss-20b with Unsloth and running it in Ollama
articles.excerpt: Originally published on khadim.tech. In short: gpt-oss-20b fine-tunes with QLoRA on a single consumer GPU (Unsloth puts it at about 14 GB of VRAM). Shipping it is where the chat template matters: gpt-…
articles.body: Originally published on khadim.tech . In short: gpt-oss-20b fine-tunes with QLoRA on a single consumer GPU (Unsloth puts it at about 14 GB of VRAM). Shipping it is where the chat template matters: gpt-oss uses OpenAI's Harmony format, so the GGUF needs a Harmony template with <|return|> as a stop token, or Ollama gives gibberish or never stops. I fine-tuned gpt-oss-20b for STEM reasoning and published it three ways: a LoRA adapter, a merged 16-bit model and GGUF files. Below are the settings and versions behind it, the export code, and the Modelfile that makes the GGUF behave in Ollama.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass TrailQuest is a screen-free, audio-guided outdoor exploration app designed for runners and walkers. Once you sel…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built TrailQuest is a screen-free, audio-guided outdoor exploration app designed for runners and walkers. Once you select your desired distance and preferences (parks, green spaces, landmarks), the backend generates a closed-loop route originating from your current location. It translates OSRM turn-by-turn navigation into spoken audio cues, keeping your attention off your phone and focused on your surroundings. During each route, participants encounter interactive activities: Visual Quests: Capture a photo of designated landmarks; an open-weight vision model validates presence and alignment. Social Quests: Greet individuals encountered along the trail to earn completion points.

articles.title: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.excerpt: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission,…
articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.

articles.body: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity. The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel .
